language: maths

Every computer has the same five kinds of parts, each with its own job. This one is a games console.

## Predict: where's my saved game?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing to which part keeps a saved game tests the new move: storage keeps things with the power off; memory doesn't."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "You save your game and turn the console off. Tomorrow, your saved game is still there. Which part kept it?"
  options: ["Storage", "Memory", "The screen", "The buttons"]
  actual: "Storage. It keeps things when the power is off. Memory only holds what the console is using while it's on."
```

## Try: match the jobs

```step
stage: run
insight: "Matching each part to its job settles the prediction and puts a job on every part. Students can press the buttons to test their guesses."
try: { playground: board, starter: "parts.yml#run", height: 520 }
check: { type: board, text: "Match each part to its job. Press the buttons on the console if it helps you decide.", when: "k = 5", explain: "Buttons take in what you do, the processor works out what happens, memory holds the score right now, storage keeps the save, the screen shows the result." }
```

Was your guess right?

## Worked example: one game, five parts

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Naming the part behind each thing that happens in a game models the move. Sam treats memory and storage as one, the mistake planted after the method."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "You press A. Which part works out that the score should go up?"
      options: ["The processor", "The buttons", "The screen", "Storage"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "The buttons only take in the press.", "The screen only shows what it's given.", "Storage only keeps things."]
      explain: "The processor follows the game's instructions: press A, add one to the score."
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "working.txt#sam"
      text: "Sam explains memory and storage. Click the line where it first goes wrong."
      answer: 3
      fault: logic
      misconception: ram-is-storage
      explain: "Line 3: they are different parts. Memory holds what's being used right now and empties when the power goes off. Storage keeps things with the power off."
```

### Five parts, five jobs

```worked
\text{Buttons (input)} :: Take in what you do: press A.
\text{Processor} :: Works out what happens: the score goes up by one.
\text{Memory} :: Holds the score while you play. It empties when the power goes off.
\text{Storage} :: Keeps the saved game when the power is off.
\text{Screen (output)} :: Shows the result: the new score.
```

Now: which part works out what happens?

### Find the mistake

## Vary: memory or storage?

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Each task does one thing to the console and watches memory and storage: play, save and restart, then load."
try: { playground: board, starter: "parts.yml#modify", height: 520 }
tasks:
  - check: { type: board, text: "Press A three times. Which part is holding the score now?", when: "a = 1 and m = 3", explain: "Memory: it holds the score while you play." }
  - check: { type: board, text: "Save the game, then turn the console off and on. What's left?", when: "a = 3 and g >= 1", explain: "Memory is back to 0, but storage still has the saved score." }
  - check: { type: board, text: "Load the game.", when: "a = 4 and o = 1", explain: "The saved score goes from storage back into memory, and the screen shows it." }
```

## Practise: which part?

```step
stage: practise
insight: "The same five kinds of parts on other devices, and a review of letter codes."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "On a laptop, which part is the keyboard?"
      options: ["Input", "Output", "Storage", "The processor"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "It takes in, it doesn't show.", "It doesn't keep anything.", "It doesn't work anything out."]
      explain: "It takes in what you type."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Your phone's photos are still there after it goes flat. Where are they kept?"
      options: ["Storage", "Memory", "The screen", "The camera"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Memory empties when the power goes off.", "The screen only shows them.", "The camera is input: it takes the photo in."]
      explain: "Storage keeps things when the power is off."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Which of these is output?"
      options: ["A speaker", "A microphone", "A mouse", "A touch on the screen"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "A microphone takes sound in.", "A mouse takes in your movements.", "Touching takes in what you do."]
      explain: "A speaker plays the result. (A touch screen is both: it takes in touches and shows the picture.)"
```

## Make: play but can't save

```step
stage: make
insight: "Taking out the one part that stops saving but not playing reverses the move: students choose the part from its job."
try: { playground: board, starter: "parts.yml#make", height: 560 }
hint: ["Which part's only job is keeping things when the power is off?", "Take that part out, press A, then try to save."]
check: { type: board, text: "Take out one part so you can still play, but you can't save. Then try to save.", when: "z = 4 and r = 1 and a = 2 and o = 0", explain: "Without storage the game still runs (memory holds the score), but there's nowhere to keep a save." }
```

Then: look at a device at home. Can you find each of the five kinds of part?

```teacher
summary: Students match the five parts of a games console to their jobs, follow
  a game through them, see memory empty and storage keep a save when the console
  is turned off and on, and take out the one part that stops saving but not
  playing (AC9TDI6K01 node 1).
time: 40
timing: Predict and Try 8 min · Worked example 8 min · Vary 9 min · Practise and
  Make 15 min
goals:
  - I can name the five kinds of parts in a computer and their jobs.
  - I can explain the difference between memory and storage.
  - I can find the same parts in a laptop or a phone.
struggle: "Memory and storage both 'remember'. Use Turn off and on every time it
  comes up: memory empties, storage keeps."
before: >
  Do the boards yourself first: press A, save, turn off and on, load.


  The one idea: five kinds of parts, one job each, and memory (empties without
  power) is not storage (keeps without power).


  Simplifications (say so if asked): one processor, one memory and one storage;
  no operating system; the game itself also sits in storage and is loaded into
  memory to run.


  Year 7–8 catch-up: Inside a computer (8K01) starts at specifications. A
  student who can say which part keeps a saved game and which empties can start
  there.


  Unplugged: five students as the parts, passing a card that says "score"
  between them.
running:
  - "Predict: students who chose memory are the lesson; don't correct yet."
  - "Try: ask pairs to test one guess on the console before they match it."
  - "Vary: before Turn off and on, ask what will be left in memory and in
    storage."
  - "Make: ask why the game still runs with no storage."
stuck:
  - see: A student says memory and storage are the same (Sam's mistake).
    ask: Press Turn off and on. Which one is empty now?
    fix: Memory empties; storage keeps.
  - see: A student says the screen does the work.
    ask: Take the screen out and press A. What happens to the score in memory?
    fix: It still goes up; the screen only shows it.
stretch: A phone is both a computer and a camera. Which of its parts are input,
  and which are output?
support: "A card with five boxes: Input (takes in), Processor (works out),
  Memory (now), Storage (keeps), Output (shows)."
leads: |
  Next: Working together (the order the parts take turns).

  Year 7–8: Inside a computer › What the specs mean.
exit:
  q: Which part holds your score while you play, and which keeps it when you turn
    off?
  a: Memory; storage.
explain: >
  Every computer has five kinds of parts. **Input** takes in what you do. The
  **processor** works out what happens. **Memory** holds what's being used right
  now. **Storage** keeps things when the power is off. **Output** shows or plays
  the result.


  Memory and storage both remember, but only storage keeps things when you turn
  the computer off.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Memory and storage both remember things. Why would a computer need both?
    prompts:
      - What happens to each when the power goes off?
      - Which one would you want your saved game in? Which one is the game using
        right now?
    notes: Memory empties when the power goes off but is fast for what's being used
      now; storage keeps things with the power off. This is the confusion that
      lasts into Year 9, so return to it at the Vary step's Turn off and on.
  activities:
    - at: start
      kind: activity
      title: Five parts, five people
      minutes: 5
      do: >
        Five volunteers wear labels: Buttons, Processor, Memory, Storage,
        Screen. Someone 'presses A': pass a card saying SCORE 1 along the right
        people.
      notes: Buttons to Processor, Processor writes the score on Memory's card,
        Processor tells Screen. Keep the five for Working together.
    - at: predict
      kind: discussion
      title: Where's my saved game?
      minutes: 2
      do: |
        Point to the volunteer who keeps your saved game overnight.
      notes: "Students pointing at Memory are the lesson. Don't correct yet: the Try
        board shows it."
    - at: modify
      kind: activity
      title: Turn off and on
      minutes: 2
      do: >
        'Power off!' Memory wipes their card clean. Storage keeps theirs. 'Power
        on!' What's left?
      notes: Do this before students press Turn off and on on the site, so the board
        confirms what they just saw.
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: Which part?
      type: question
      q: Which part takes in what you do?
      options:
        - Input
        - Output
        - Memory
        - Storage
      answer: 0
      explain: "Input: buttons, a keyboard, a touch screen, a microphone."
```
